ALL.text:
Allstate's #3 ranking is anchored by an exceptionally strong Value score of 94.5, and the raw multiples back this up: a P/E of 5.33, P/FCF of 5.62, and P/S under 1.0 all point to a business the market is pricing cheaply relative to its earnings and cash generation. That value case is reinforced by genuinely high-quality profitability — ROE of 42.71% and ROIC of 33.52% are standout figures, low debt (Debt/Equity of 0.24), and a Piotroski F-Score of 8/9, signaling broad-based financial health. Quality lands at a solid 62.2 despite those metrics, likely because insurers screen differently on some ratios. Growth (58.7) is respectable, helped by 203.78% EPS growth year-over-year and a 44.69% earnings surprise, though revenue only grew 4.4%.

That gap is the first thing worth scrutinizing. The triple-digit EPS growth and low P/E reflect a rebound in underwriting profitability — insurance earnings swing sharply with catastrophe losses and premium repricing, so a 5x P/E built on a recovery year can look cheaper than a normalized earnings base would justify. The huge earnings surprise suggests the recovery outpaced expectations, which is hard to repeat. Momentum is the clear laggard at 48.9, roughly middle-of-the-pack, meaning the market hasn't rewarded these results with strong price strength — often a sign investors doubt the earnings are durable. A reader should check whether current profitability is cyclically elevated, how exposed the book is to catastrophe seasons, and whether that 4.4% top-line growth can sustain the earnings.

GOOG.text:
Alphabet lands at #10 overall with a balanced profile led by Quality (66.7) and Momentum (68.4), supported by Growth (61.3), and held back by Value (26.2). The quality reading is well earned: ROE of 38.98% and ROIC of 35.11% point to highly efficient capital deployment, while gross margin of 60.37%, operating margin of 32.69%, and net margin of 37.92% reflect the economics of a dominant search and advertising franchise. The balance sheet is fortress-like — debt/equity of just 0.16, a current ratio of 1.92, and an extraordinary Altman Z-Score of 16.86 signal minimal financial risk. Growth is genuine too, with revenue up 17.45% and EPS up a striking 48.51% year over year.

The Value factor is the clear drag, and the multiples explain why: a P/E of 27.14, P/B of 7.26, P/S of 10.29, and especially a P/FCF of 67.49 leave little margin for error at a $4.3 trillion market cap. That lofty price-to-free-cash-flow figure sits awkwardly against FCF growth of only 0.7% — a sharp contrast to the headline EPS growth, suggesting heavy capital spending (likely AI and data-center investment) is consuming cash even as accounting earnings surge.

Readers should note the momentum score reflects a strong run that may already price in optimism, and the latest earnings surprise was slightly negative (-3.15%). The Piotroski F-Score of 6/9 is solid but not exceptional. Worth checking whether cash generation reaccelerates or capex continues to outpace it.

ANET.text:
Arista's #3 ranking rests on a strong combination of Momentum (77.8) and Quality (75.2), with Growth (63.2) providing support. The quality signal is well-earned: return on equity and return on invested capital both sit at roughly 30.6%, gross margin is 63.5%, operating margin 42.8%, and net margin 38.3% — figures that point to a highly profitable networking business with genuine pricing power. Notably, debt/equity is zero and the current ratio is 2.83, so this profitability isn't leverage-assisted; the balance sheet is clean. Growth reinforces the picture, with revenue up 30.6% year-over-year, EPS up 23.5%, and a 5.79% earnings surprise suggesting the business is still exceeding expectations.

The obvious counterweight is Value, scoring just 13.9. Every headline multiple is elevated — a P/E of 63.3, P/S of 24.3, P/B of 11.4, and P/FCF of 44.6. The market is already pricing in continued rapid expansion, which means the strong momentum score comes with the usual caveat: a stock riding a sustained run late in the cycle can reverse sharply if growth decelerates or a single earnings report disappoints.

A reader should double-check whether that 30% revenue growth is sustainable, given Arista's heavy exposure to a concentrated set of large cloud/hyperscaler customers — customer concentration can make growth lumpy. Also worth noting is that EPS growth (23.5%) trails revenue growth (30.6%), a small sign margins may be under pressure. At these valuations, the numbers leave little room for a stumble.

CFG.text:
Citizens Financial Group's #8 rank and 57.5 score are built primarily on its Value factor (82.4), the standout among its scores. That's easy to see in the metrics: a P/B of 0.98 means the market is pricing the bank essentially at book value, while the P/E of 15.06 and P/FCF of 10.81 are unremarkable rather than expensive. Growth (69) and Momentum (61.3) provide secondary support — headline revenue growth of 62.73% and EPS growth of 31.85% look striking, and a perfect Piotroski F-Score of 9/9 signals broad fundamental improvement across profitability, leverage, and efficiency measures. The 2.81% earnings surprise adds a modest positive.

The clear weak link is Quality at 25.8, which is what pulls the final score down despite three respectable factors. The reason is visible in returns: ROE of 7.63% and ROIC of 5.47% are thin, suggesting the bank isn't generating strong returns on its capital base — which also helps explain why it trades below book value. A reader should treat that sub-1.0 P/B as a signal to check, not a bargain to assume: the market may be discounting the low return profile or credit/interest-rate concerns rather than mispricing the stock.

Also worth scrutinizing is the 62.73% revenue growth, an outsized figure for a bank that likely reflects rate-cycle or acquisition/base effects rather than organic sustainability. For financials, many standard quality gauges (gross margin, current ratio, Altman Z) are n/a, so the Quality read leans heavily on those modest return metrics.

LLY.text:
Eli Lilly's #14 ranking and 54.2 final score are built almost entirely on the growth and quality side of the model. Growth scores an exceptional 86.8, backed by 47.4% year-over-year revenue growth, 128.8% EPS growth, 90.7% FCF growth, and a 27% earnings surprise — figures consistent with the surge in demand for its GLP-1 franchise. Quality is also strong at 67.9, supported by an eye-watering 101% ROE, 37.7% ROIC, an 82.8% gross margin, and a 43.6% operating margin, plus a solid Piotroski score of 7/9. This is a business converting sales into profit at elite rates. Momentum sits mid-pack at 56.9, suggesting the price run has cooled somewhat rather than accelerating.

The overwhelming drag is Value, at just 8.8 — near the bottom of the universe. Investors are paying 44x earnings, 27.9x book, 15.5x sales, and a striking 108x free cash flow. Those multiples price in continued rapid growth, so the valuation offers little cushion if revenue or earnings decelerate, or if competitive and regulatory pressures on obesity drugs intensify.

A reader should note the ROE of 101% is inflated by leverage — debt/equity sits at 1.39, so headline returns partly reflect a thinner equity base, not just operational excellence. The P/FCF of 108 also flags that free cash flow lags reported earnings, worth checking against heavy capacity investment. Finally, growth this steep is difficult to sustain; the model rewards the trailing numbers, not whether that 47% pace can repeat.

ADI.text:
Analog Devices lands at #16 with a final score of 53.4, and the ranking is clearly powered by its Momentum (83.6) and Growth (77.9) factors. The growth story is concrete: revenue is up 29.75% year-over-year, EPS has jumped 83.19%, and free cash flow grew 37%, with a recent 5.33% earnings surprise reinforcing the upward trend. The business itself shows genuine quality in its margin structure — a 64.49% gross margin, 32.5% operating margin, and 26.01% net margin are strong for a semiconductor company — and a Piotroski F-Score of 8/9 signals healthy fundamental momentum. Leverage is modest, with debt/equity at 0.26 and a current ratio of 1.75.

The tension lies in the two weaker factors. Value scores just 19.3, and the multiples explain why: a P/E of 58, P/S of 15.13, P/B of 5.74, and P/FCF of 42 all price ADI as an expensive stock. Quality is only middling at 40.3 despite those fat margins, because returns on capital are thin — ROE of 9.79% and ROIC of 7.79% are unremarkable, and gross profit/assets of 14.1% suggests a heavy, capital-intensive balance sheet.

A reader should weigh a few things. The eye-catching EPS and revenue growth likely reflect recovery off a cyclical trough, so those rates may not be sustainable — semiconductor demand is notoriously cyclical. High momentum can also arrive late in a run. And a rich valuation leaves little cushion if growth decelerates or ROIC stays subdued relative to the price being paid.

TER.text:
Teradyne's #9 ranking is overwhelmingly a momentum story, with a near-top-decile momentum score of 96.7 doing most of the heavy lifting. That's backed by real fundamental strength: revenue grew 30.3% year-over-year, EPS jumped 52.9%, and the latest earnings surprise of 20.5% suggests the business is beating expectations as the semiconductor test cycle turns. Quality is solid at 59.3, supported by a 29.7% ROE, 28.7% ROIC, and healthy margins (58.7% gross, 26.5% operating). The balance sheet is pristine — essentially zero debt, a 2.15 current ratio, and an Altman Z-Score of 26.1 that signals virtually no bankruptcy risk. Growth at 66.8 rounds out a picture of a profitable, expanding, financially sound company.

The glaring weakness is Value, scoring just 4.7 — near the bottom of the universe. Investors are paying a steep price for that growth and momentum: a P/E of 65.9, P/B of 13.76, P/S of 14.87, and a P/FCF above 100. Those multiples leave little margin for error if growth decelerates.

A reader should double-check a few tensions. First, the momentum score is very high, which often comes late in a run and can reverse sharply in cyclical semiconductor names. Second, despite strong EPS growth, free cash flow actually fell 5%, and the Piotroski F-Score of 6/9 is only moderate — worth reconciling against the rosy income-statement figures. Finally, the rich valuation means much of the good news may already be priced in.

PNC.text:
PNC's #17 ranking and 53.4 composite are anchored by its Value factor (73.4), the standout among its four scores. On the surface the valuation is undemanding: a P/E of 14.0, P/B of 1.31, and P/FCF of 14.8 are modest for a large-cap bank, and a 28.83% net margin alongside a 34.54% operating margin reflects the typically high-margin economics of a diversified financial institution. Growth (55.2) and Momentum (51.1) both sit near the middle of the pack, so the stock is neither leading nor lagging on price trend, while reported revenue growth of 72.27% is eye-catching and helps the Growth reading.

The clear drag is Quality at 37.6, the weakest factor and a meaningful counterweight given Quality carries the largest weight in the model. ROE of 11.98% and ROIC of just 6.89% are unremarkable, and the Debt/Equity of 0.71 reflects the leverage inherent to a bank's balance sheet — worth noting that many quality sub-metrics (Altman Z, Piotroski, current ratio, gross margin) read "n/a," which is normal for financials but means the Quality score rests on a thinner set of inputs.

A reader should scrutinize the growth figures: 72.27% revenue growth is unusually large and likely reflects accounting or comparison-base quirks common in bank revenue, not sustainable organic expansion. It also sits against a -44.4% decline in free cash flow, a divergence worth understanding. The near-flat 0.84% earnings surprise suggests results are landing broadly in line with expectations rather than accelerating.

PFG.text:
Principal Financial Group's #13 ranking (54.8/100) is anchored by its Value score of 81.6, comfortably its strongest factor. The valuation metrics support this: a P/E of 15.52, P/B of 1.65, P/S of 1.57 and an especially cheap-looking P/FCF of 6.68 all point to a stock that is not richly priced relative to its earnings and cash generation. Momentum at 65.1 is respectable, suggesting price action has been supportive, and the modest 2.26% earnings surprise indicates the business is roughly meeting expectations. Working against these are Quality (35) and Growth (38.2), both below the midpoint. ROE of 13.35% and ROIC of 9.98% are decent but not standout for a financial, and the Piotroski F-Score of 6/9 is middling. Leverage is conservative, with Debt/Equity at 0.33.

A reader should weigh what the value score may be masking. Revenue growth is slightly negative (-1.76%) and FCF growth is also down (-1.4%), so the low valuation partly reflects a business that isn't expanding at the top line. The eye-catching 50.05% EPS growth likely reflects one-off or base-effect factors rather than durable operating momentum, given flat revenue — worth checking against reported results. Many balance-sheet and margin fields (gross margin, Debt/EBITDA, Altman Z, current ratio) are "n/a," typical for an insurer/asset manager, meaning some standard quality checks simply don't translate here. The net effect is a cheap, moderately stable financial whose weak growth and average quality temper the appeal of its valuation.

TROW.text:
T Rowe Price's #20 rank rests primarily on its Value and Quality scores. On valuation, a P/E of 12.13, P/B of 1.82, and P/FCF of 14.3 place it in the 73rd percentile — a reflection of the market pricing the asset manager conservatively. Quality (67.3) is backed by genuinely strong profitability: ROE of 19.48% and ROIC of 19.42% are healthy, operating margin sits at 30.73%, net margin at 28.28%, and the balance sheet carries zero debt with a current ratio of 3.64. The near-100% gross margin is characteristic of an asset manager, where fee revenue carries almost no cost of goods. Free cash flow growth of 17.2% and a 4.97% earnings surprise add support.

The drag comes from Momentum (26.7) and Growth (33.2). Revenue grew just 4.23% and EPS 5.66% year over year — modest for a business whose earnings are tethered to assets under management. The weak momentum score suggests the stock has lagged, which is worth pairing with the cheap valuation: a low P/E can signal value or can reflect investors' skepticism about future fee income.

Readers should double-check what the low multiple is discounting. Asset managers face structural pressure from fee compression and outflows toward passive products, so the modest revenue growth may not be a one-off. The zero-debt, high-margin profile is attractive, but sustainability of AUM-driven earnings — and whether the FCF growth is repeatable versus a favorable market year — deserves scrutiny before reading the value score as a bargain.

MU.text:
Micron's #5 ranking is powered almost entirely by its Momentum (100) and Growth (98.7) scores, both sitting at or near the top of the ranked universe. The growth figures are extraordinary: revenue up 167% year-over-year, EPS up roughly 700%, and free cash flow up over 1,278%, alongside a 17.3% earnings surprise. Quality is also strong at 74.7, supported by a 70.6% ROE, 61.5% ROIC, and margins that are exceptional for a hardware business — 72.6% gross, 65.6% operating, and 55.9% net. The balance sheet reinforces this: debt/equity of just 0.06, debt/EBITDA of 0.8, a current ratio of 3.42, an Altman Z-Score of 25, and a Piotroski F-Score of 8/9. Value is the clear laggard at 34.4, and a large insider-selling penalty (-15) is the single biggest drag on the final 60.8.

A reader should weigh a few things. Momentum pinned at exactly 100 means the stock is at the top of its run, so the score reflects how far it has already moved, not where it goes next. The growth rates are lapping unusually depressed prior-year comparisons — triple-digit expansion is unlikely to repeat, and future quarters will face far tougher year-over-year math. Valuation multiples (P/B 10.3, P/S 12.3, P/FCF 42) already embed rich expectations, explaining the weak Value score. Finally, the heavy insider selling against this backdrop is worth investigating directly, as it partly offsets the otherwise strong quality and growth signals.

HST.text:
Host Hotels' #7 ranking (final score 59.9) leans most heavily on Momentum, its strongest factor at 76.9, backed by a striking 59.43% earnings surprise and EPS growth of 51.77% year-over-year. Value is the next contributor at 66, supported by reasonable multiples for a REIT: a P/E of 15.7, P/B of 1.93, and P/FCF around 17. The balance sheet reads conservatively for the sector — debt/equity of 0.74 and debt/EBITDA of just 0.77 are low for a hotel-focused real estate company, and a Piotroski F-Score of 8/9 signals broad fundamental improvement across profitability, leverage, and efficiency. Quality (46) and Growth (52) are middling, keeping the overall score from climbing higher.

A few things sit beneath these numbers. The 96.89% gross margin is characteristic of REIT accounting and shouldn't be read as unusual pricing power; the operating margin of 18.35% and net margin of 16.4% are the more meaningful profitability reads. ROIC of 8.6% versus ROE of 15.16% shows leverage is doing some of the work behind returns. The eye-catching EPS growth (51.77%) and earnings surprise (59.43%) are worth contextualizing — hotel earnings are cyclical and can rebound sharply off soft comparisons, so a reader should check whether that momentum reflects durable demand or an easy prior-year base. FCF growth of just 0.8% contrasts sharply with EPS growth, hinting the bottom-line jump isn't yet flowing through to cash. The modest Quality and Growth scores temper the momentum story.

INCY.text:
Incyte tops the ranked universe on the strength of its Growth factor (87.1), which reflects genuinely striking momentum in the fundamentals: 21.5% year-over-year revenue growth, FCF growth of 321%, and an EPS growth figure of 2,455% — the latter almost certainly a base-effect distortion off a depressed prior-year number rather than a repeatable rate. Quality is the second pillar (71.5), and here the business looks structurally sound: gross margins near 93%, operating margin of 30%, ROE and ROIC both around 29%, and a pristine balance sheet with essentially no debt (D/E 0.01), a 3.68 current ratio, and an Altman Z-Score of 9.92 signaling negligible financial distress risk. Value (60.7) is respectable rather than cheap, with a P/E of 16.3 and P/FCF of 16.1 — reasonable for a profitable biopharma. The Piotroski F-Score of 7/9 rounds out a solid fundamental picture with no penalties applied.

What the numbers may obscure: the headline growth rates are inflated by low comparison bases, so a reader should check whether normalized earnings and cash flow growth are sustainable or one-off. The 29.4% earnings surprise similarly suggests the market was positioned for weaker results, which can cut both ways. Momentum at 59 is the softest factor, hinting price has not fully confirmed the fundamental strength. Biopharma-specific risks — patent cliffs (notably Jakafi concentration), pipeline dependence, and regulatory outcomes — sit outside this quantitative frame and warrant separate scrutiny, since a single drug's trajectory can reshape these clean ratios quickly.

FFIV.text:
F5's #15 ranking and 53.9 final score are carried primarily by Momentum (74.9), with a solid but unspectacular Quality reading (58.7) providing support. The Momentum strength reflects recent share performance and a 10.63% earnings surprise, suggesting the stock has been rewarding holders and beating expectations. On the Quality side the business looks genuinely clean: an 81.5% gross margin, ~22% net margin, ROE and ROIC both near 20%, zero debt on the balance sheet, and a Piotroski F-Score of 8/9 all point to a highly profitable, self-funding software/hardware operation with little financial risk. Growth is middling at 46.9, though the underlying numbers are respectable — 9.7% revenue growth, 15.7% EPS growth, and 18.9% FCF growth, with earnings outpacing sales thanks to margin discipline and buyback-friendly economics.

The clear drag is Value at 32.8. At a P/E of 34.3, P/S of 7.5, and P/B of 4.5, the market is already paying a premium multiple, so much of the quality and momentum appears priced in. A reader should weigh whether the 74.9 Momentum score reflects a run that is maturing — high momentum late in a cycle can reverse quickly, and pairing it with a rich valuation raises sensitivity to any earnings disappointment. Also check that the ~10% top-line growth justifies a 34x multiple, and whether the 21.96% net margin and single-digit revenue growth can sustain the double-digit EPS growth the momentum story leans on.

CINF.text:
Cincinnati Financial's #6 ranking (60.2/100) is powered chiefly by its Value factor, which sits at a strong 90th percentile. The underlying multiples back this up: a P/E of roughly 10, P/B of 1.56, P/S of 2.13 and P/FCF near 8 all point to a modestly priced insurer. Growth is the second pillar at 73.5, reflecting 18.8% year-over-year revenue growth, 17.7% FCF growth, and an eye-catching 90.8% EPS jump. Profitability looks solid too, with ROE of 18% and ROIC of 17%, a 21% net margin, and almost no leverage (debt/equity of 0.05). Together these paint a picture of a well-capitalized, cheaply valued business firing on its top line.

The offsets sit in Quality (52.2, merely average) and especially Momentum (29.2, weak), meaning the share price has lagged even as fundamentals improved. That divergence is worth examining: a low momentum score alongside a high value score can signal either an unloved bargain or a market pricing in headwinds the trailing numbers don't yet show.

A reader should be cautious about the 90.8% EPS growth — for a property-casualty insurer, huge earnings swings often reflect investment-portfolio gains or favorable claims/catastrophe experience rather than durable operating improvement, which can reverse in a bad-loss year. The low P/E may partly be flattering off that inflated base. The Piotroski F-Score of 6/9 is decent but not exceptional, and the "average" Quality score suggests the standout ROE and margins deserve a look at how much is underwriting versus market-driven.

NTAP.text:
NetApp's #4 ranking is powered chiefly by Momentum (88.5), which sits near the top of the universe, alongside a solid Quality score (67.5). The quality picture is genuinely strong: gross margins of 70.7%, operating margins of 24.2%, and a striking ROIC of 35.4% point to an efficient, profitable storage-and-data business. The Piotroski F-Score of 8/9 signals broadly improving fundamentals, and the Altman Z-Score of 3.42 places the firm outside distress territory. FCF growth of 39.7% year over year and a recent 5.1% earnings surprise help explain the momentum reading.

Pulling the other way are Value (45.1) and Growth (44), both middling. The P/E of 25.9 and P/S of 4.78 are not cheap, and revenue growth of just 5.4% is modest — the double-digit EPS growth (11.9%) leans on margins and buybacks more than top-line expansion. That combination is worth watching: momentum scores this high late in a run can reverse if the market's expectations reset.

A reader should also scrutinize the balance sheet framing behind that eye-catching 114% ROE. Debt/Equity of 1.84 and a P/B of 15.88 indicate a thin equity base — heavy buybacks flatter ROE and per-share metrics without the underlying business necessarily earning that return on true capital. Debt/EBITDA of 1.34 is manageable, so leverage looks serviceable rather than alarming. In short, a high-quality, richly-priced name where the momentum and profitability signals deserve to be checked against slow revenue growth and an equity-light capital structure.

STT.text:
State Street's #2 ranking (final score 68) is built primarily on three of the four pillars: Value (83.4), Momentum (81.8), and Growth (74.9). On valuation, the stock looks inexpensive across multiple lenses — a P/E of 16.27, P/B of just 1.26, and an especially low P/FCF of 2.54, which suggests strong free-cash generation relative to its $50B market cap. The Growth score is flattered by eye-catching year-over-year figures: revenue up 181% and FCF up 177%. Momentum near 82 indicates the shares have been performing well recently, and a 7.76% earnings surprise reinforces that near-term operating results have been beating expectations. Margins are healthy for a financial, with a 24.96% operating margin and 20.5% net margin.

The clear laggard is Quality at 38.9, and that weak factor deserves scrutiny. ROE of 11.09% is modest, and ROIC of just 5.04% is low, hinting that the business isn't generating especially high returns on the capital it deploys. Debt/Equity of 1.09 reflects meaningful leverage, though this is typical for a custody bank. Note also that the headline growth numbers are suspect: 181% revenue growth is not organic for an established bank and likely reflects an accounting or comparison-base distortion — EPS grew a far more modest 11.47%, which is a better guide to real earnings progress. Readers should also weigh how much of the Momentum score reflects an already-extended run, and check whether the cheap P/FCF holds up under normalized cash-flow definitions.

USB.text:
US Bancorp's #19 ranking and 52.6 score are carried almost entirely by Value, which sits at a strong 84.6 percentile. The supporting metrics back that up: a P/E of 12.45, P/B of 1.23, P/S of 2.1 and P/FCF of roughly 10 all point to a bank trading at modest multiples relative to peers. Growth (53.1) and Momentum (46.1) are middling, while Quality is the clear laggard at 31.1. That Quality weakness is the tension in this profile — with Quality carrying the heaviest 30% weight in the model, a sub-average score meaningfully caps the final result even as the cheap valuation lifts it.

Drilling into Quality, ROE of 12.21% is respectable for a bank but ROIC of just 5.49% is thin, and Debt/Equity of 1.2 reflects the leverage inherent to the financials sector (though leverage metrics are less comparable for banks). The 84% year-over-year revenue growth looks eye-catching but is almost certainly distorted by acquisition or accounting effects rather than organic expansion — worth checking against the far more modest 17% EPS growth, which is a cleaner signal of actual earnings power.

A reader should also weigh the -29.8% FCF decline, which sits uneasily against the healthy 20% net margin and cheap P/FCF, and note that many standard screens (Piotroski, Altman Z, current ratio) are not applicable to banks. The low valuation may reflect genuine market skepticism about credit quality or rate exposure rather than a simple bargain, so the "why is it cheap" question deserves scrutiny.

MTB.text:
M&T Bank's #12 ranking (final score 55.1) is anchored by a strong Value factor of 84.6, supported by cheap-looking multiples: a P/E of 12.11, P/B of just 1.09, and P/FCF around 11.2. These are typical of a regional bank trading close to book value, and the 30.7% net margin plus 40.6% operating margin show a profitable, well-run lender. Growth scores a respectable 60.2, helped by eye-catching 86% year-over-year revenue growth and 19.4% EPS growth, while a perfect Piotroski F-Score of 9/9 signals clean, improving fundamentals across profitability, leverage, and efficiency trends.

What holds the overall score back are Quality (38.8) and Momentum (41.1). Despite the flawless F-Score, headline returns are modest: ROE of 10.25% and ROIC of 6.66% are unremarkable and below what higher-quality franchises generate, which explains why the market only pays roughly book value. The middling momentum reading suggests the stock has not been a standout performer recently, so the "value" here may reflect market skepticism rather than a pure bargain.

A reader should scrutinize a few things. That 86% revenue growth figure is unusually large for an established bank and likely reflects acquisition effects or accounting/comparison distortions — check whether it's organic. FCF growth is actually negative (-16.8%), diverging from the EPS story. Standard bank caveats also apply: metrics like current ratio, gross margin, and Altman Z are n/a, and Debt/Equity of 0.68 tells you little about credit quality, loan-book risk, or interest-rate exposure.

GOOGL.text:
Alphabet's #11 rank rests on a broad-based profile with no single dominant factor and no penalties. Momentum leads at 70.3, reflecting a strong price run, while Quality (64.9) is anchored by genuinely exceptional profitability: 38.98% ROE, 35.11% ROIC, 60.37% gross margins and a near-38% net margin. The balance sheet reinforces this — debt/equity of just 0.16 and an Altman Z-Score of 16.86 signal minimal financial risk. Growth (59.7) is respectable, with 17.45% revenue growth and a striking 48.51% EPS jump, suggesting operating leverage and margin expansion beyond top-line gains. The clear laggard is Value at 24.6, which pulls the final score down and explains why a business this high-quality doesn't rank higher.

The Value weakness is worth understanding: a P/E of 27, P/B of 7.26, P/S above 10, and especially a P/FCF near 67 mean the market already prices in substantial future growth. That P/FCF figure sits oddly against near-flat FCF growth (0.7%) despite the 48.5% EPS surge — a gap readers should probe, as it may reflect heavy capital spending (data centers, AI infrastructure) eating into cash conversion. The Piotroski F-Score of 6/9 is solid but not pristine, and the latest earnings surprise was slightly negative (-3.15%), a reminder that momentum can run ahead of fundamentals. In short, this is a high-quality, richly-valued name where the strong ROE and margins are real, but the elevated multiples and stalled free cash flow deserve scrutiny before drawing conclusions.

FDX.text:
FedEx lands at #18 largely on the strength of its Momentum (81.1) and Value (65.4) scores, which more than offset weaker Quality (31.9) and Growth (35.1). The momentum reading suggests the shares have been climbing relative to peers, while the value case rests on undemanding multiples: a P/E of 16.75, P/S of just 0.82, and P/FCF around 17. For a logistics business of this scale, that combination flags a stock the market is pricing conservatively even as recent earnings beat expectations by 4.78% and EPS grew 17.85% year-over-year.

The quality and growth picture is more sober. Operating margin of 6.2% and net margin of 4.88% are thin — the 62.6% gross margin doesn't survive the heavy cost of running a physical delivery network. ROIC of 8.88% is modest against a Debt/Equity of 0.85 and Debt/EBITDA of 2.1, and the Piotroski F-Score of 6/9 is middling. Revenue grew only 4.69%, so the strong EPS growth appears driven more by cost discipline and buybacks than by expansion.

A reader should weigh a few things. The high momentum score can arrive late in a run, so it's worth checking whether the recent move already reflects the earnings optimism. FCF actually shrank 4.9%, which sits awkwardly against the appealing P/FCF headline. And the low quality/growth scores mean two of four factors are working against the ranking — this is a cheap, moving stock, not a high-return compounder on these numbers.
